source.title: More findings on Memorization and double descent

record.file_problem: Whole post and comments are present. Figures are referenced but their plotted values are not included in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The post explicitly replicates a subset of Toy Models of Superposition using the toy-model setup and reports that its sparsity-dependent superposition findings match the original; it also tests related settings.
record.gate_note: The text gives qualitative summaries of several plotted experiments but not their plotted numerical results. I record the explicit prose findings, not results cited from other work. Double-descent findings, cosine-similarity observations, and final-layer results do not directly test the listed superposition or polysemanticity versions.
record.test_reason: The post replicates the original's ReLU output model sparsity sweep (n=20, m=5, I=0.7^i) and ReLU hidden model (n=10, m=5, I=0.75^i). It uses the same methods and measures (W^TW, norms, superposition metric, stack plots) and reports results that basically match.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right, but the post's main takeaways are about memorization. Double descent is consistent across settings, and the memorized dictionary is easy to read only in the simplest cases. Feature reconstruction shows regular sparsity- and importance-dependent patterns. The superposition replication is a subset. The author is unsure of the relevance to real transformers.
record.recipe_differences: Explicitly replicates a subset of the original toy-model findings, but modifies some settings in the double-descent experiments and also studies other architectures and reconstruction tasks.
record.method_sensitivity: Bias initialization changes the reported superposition results. Sparsity, importance distribution, noise, hidden size, and reconstruction setup affect reported outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: MLPs given a randomly projected sparse input (big fish, small fish, re-projector) reconstruct features with limits set mainly by hidden size. ReLU appears to make computation in superposition harder.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: ReLU MLPs are limited in computing on superposed inputs, with capacity set mainly by the number of hidden neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: Double descent and the memorization-to-generalization transition replicate in bottleneck, MLP and cross-entropy unembedding toy settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The toy-model memorization/double-descent transition is consistent across toy architectures and losses.

record.problems: Most reported outcomes are presented in figures whose numerical values are not available in the text. The author notes sensitivity to bias initialization, and the post itself cautions that the toy settings may not generalize to actual transformers.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for double-descent experiments, final-layer/unembedding experiments, cosine-similarity observations, or memorization-only findings because they do not directly measure the listed superposition/polysemanticity versions.

untested.parts: No quantitative phase-transition location, no measure of near-orthogonality, and no polytope or regular-geometry claims reported in text. Plots are said to match but are not described.
There is no direct per-feature measure of dedicated versus shared dimensions as a function of importance, beyond the stack-plot qualitative match.
Not tested: no LLMs or SAEs.

missing.what: Appendix: an MLP trained with MSE on orthogonal one-hot inputs struggles when hidden size is much lower than dataset size, unlike no-ReLU models. The author suggests 'the ReLU makes superposition harder'.
missing.locator: Appendix — Linear block, hidden size vs dataset size

record.verdict_notes: The post is primarily about memorization. Superposition results are qualitative replications whose numerical values exist only in figures. The double-descent replication targets the sequel paper, not the original source.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not report a quantitative test of how nearly orthogonal the feature directions are, or directly compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features.

The experiments report effects of importance, sparsity, and available dimensions on reconstruction, but do not directly establish that particular important features receive dedicated dimensions while less important features share them.
No alternative cause of polysemanticity is tested.
No LLM activations, neurons, or dictionary-learning/SAE features are studied.
No test of SAE features as complete, stable, or canonical units.
No comparison of one-dimensional and multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: ReLU hidden model (toy)
rows.operation_detail: Compared learned weights and superposition as sparsity varied.
rows.value: The author reports that increasing sparsity increases superposition; the weights become more convoluted and the stack plots indicate more polysemanticity.
rows.locator: MLP block — Replicating MLP section from superposition paper
rows.note: The author says the results basically match those in the cited paper.
rows.check: Also bears on V2. At zero sparsity the network forms five monosemantic neurons, and polysemanticity rises with sparsity in a privileged basis.

rows.value: Uniform importance produces worse loss but better accuracy than decreasing importance.
rows.note: The author says decreasing importance makes the network focus on fewer features and ignore the least important ones.
rows.check: Should be observed, not partial. The author says decreasing importance makes the network ignore the least important features, as the capacity account predicts.

rows.value: The sparser the vector, the better the reconstruction loss and accuracy.

rows.subject: Bottleneck ReLU output model (toy)
rows.operation_detail: Compared the number of one-hot vectors the network could recreate across reconstruction settings.
rows.measure: Number of one-hot vectors that can be recreated
rows.value: Under these rough conditions, the network recreates roughly as many one-hot vectors as it has neurons.
rows.note: The comparison is qualitative; no exact counts are supplied.
rows.check: With dense features and decreasing importance, it recreates about as many one-hot vectors as it has neurons, i.e. no superposition. This is the dense end of V1's sparsity dependence, not a partial V2 result.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V1. With decreasing importance and zero sparsity, the network recreates roughly as many one-hot vectors as it has neurons. This count alone does not establish whether feature directions overlap.

source_check.problem: The reconstruction count is accurate, but interpreting it as a direct measurement of no superposition exceeds what this measure establishes.

rows.subject: Bottleneck ReLU output model (toy)
rows.operation_detail: Compared the number of reconstructable concepts across reconstruction settings.
rows.measure: Number of concepts the network can store/reconstruct
rows.value: The author describes the number as practically unbounded.
rows.note: This is the author's qualitative characterization; no numerical capacity is given.
rows.check: The argmax-accuracy capacity in a noiseless uniform setting is the author's qualitative characterization ('practically unbounded'). It does not measure superposition geometry or the cause of polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Big fish MLP
rows.size_stated: Dataset of 1000; feature count varied; hidden size varied
rows.operation_detail: Measured reconstruction of the original input after random projection through a bottleneck.
rows.value: Bottleneck size has little effect; hidden size is the relevant factor for reconstruction loss and accuracy. The network appears unable to reverse the random projection unless given roughly as many dimensions as input features.
rows.locator: MLP block — Limits of reconstruction, big fish setting
rows.note: The post interprets this as evidence that many features can be packed into a smaller bottleneck using superposition.
rows.check: This is an MLP reconstruction after a random projection, i.e. computation in superposition. It is not toy-model storage geometry or the capacity account of polysemantic neurons.

rows.subject: Small fish ReLU model
rows.size_stated: Dataset of 1000; feature count varied; hidden size varied
rows.operation_detail: Measured reconstruction of the projected input identity.
rows.measure: Number of inputs reconstructed and reconstruction performance
rows.value: More inputs are recovered than in the big fish setting, but the model still cannot reconstruct all inputs.
rows.locator: MLP block — Limits of reconstruction, small fish setting
rows.note: The author says this suggests ReLU networks struggle more with computations in superposition than networks without a ReLU between layers.
rows.check: Same as r9: a computation-in-superposition reconstruction task, not a measure of any version.

rows.subject: Re-projector MLP
rows.size_stated: Dataset of 1000; feature count varied; hidden size varied
rows.operation_detail: Mapped one random low-rank representation to another and measured reconstruction.
rows.value: Results look pretty similar to the big fish setting; the author says reconstruction is limited primarily by hidden size.
rows.locator: MLP block — Limits of reconstruction, re-projector setting
rows.note: The post describes this as confirming Adam Jermyn's findings; those cited findings are not separately recorded here.
rows.check: Same as r9: a re-projector reconstruction task, not a measure of any version.
